Opinion 
 Nobel Prize 2026: Why Hall and Woodford’s economic research resonates in today’s world
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 13 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 This year’s Nobel Prize honours Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, whose work draws upon microeconomic studies for a macro policy framework that holds special relevance in a world of high flux and economic shocks. Hear of ‘policy reflexivity,’ think of this duo. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 This year’s Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Robert E. Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia for providing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” 
 The citation says it all: the duo developed new macro models “that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy.” Well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures based on these models “can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.” 
 As the awarding panel’s chair John Hassler noted, the laureates’ work has been of good use to central banks and governments in securing an economy from shocks like energy price spikes and sudden shifts in retail demand. 
 The interesting part this year is the award’s recognition of work that uses micro analysis—at the level of firms and households—for a macro policy framework. The important part is the resonance that research by Hall and Woodford holds in today’s world of frequent economic shocks. 
 The panel puts it well: “The stabilization of aggregate economic activity is a central goal of economic policy.” This is especially so since such flux rarely hits people evenly; both recessions and inflation hit the poor harder. 
 The relationship between key aggregate variables like inflation, unemployment and GDP were broadly mapped at a macro level, with a major role played by Keynes, best known for making a case for intervention in an economy. 
 Today, policies to smoothen economic cycles are par for the course. The trouble was that the inner workings of those links were mostly a “ black box ,” in the panel’s words. Hall and Woodford helped open it up by delving into micro theory. 
 The former focused on demand and the latter on supply. Hall found that while household buying did depend on factors like expectations of the future, changes in it were unpredictable—like a ‘random walk.’ 
 In a 1978 article, he showed that a theory of consumption-smoothing—the idea that consumers prefer to keep it stable over time—worked well for grasping movements in overall consumption captured by data. However, unforeseeable shocks implied that consumption could not be as easily manipulated by government policy as was once thought, thus potentially limiting the effects of macro policy. 
 On his part, Woodford became the key architect of the so-called New Keynesian model: a full macro stabilization framework that has become the main tool for policymakers today. 
 He studied key micro conditions that made the market mechanism rigid. Sticky prices, for example. Businesses usually do not vary prices on a daily basis as demand and supply fluctuate; instead they adjust prices in discrete steps based on various calculations. These adjustments are also forward-looking. Woodford examined micro-level behaviour and used its learnings to formulate his new model for the use of policy tools. 
 While his original work was meant to sharpen monetary-policy analysis, the foundation it laid became a major tool for the analysis of fiscal policy as well. 
 The duo’s work can be said to have inspired today’s market notion of ‘reflexivity’ or awkward feedback loops adding complexity to macro policies. 
 Together, this year’s winners showed how aptly used fiscal and monetary policy can improve welfare by acting as a shock absorber. At a time of high uncertainty, with folks worried about the ability of authorities to cushion hard blows, the academic exertions of Hall and Woodford deserve policy-level attention.

 About the Author
 Mint Editorial Board 
 The Mint Editorial Board is a panel of editorial writers with expertise across diverse domains of relevance to the newspaper’s opinion readers. The Board draws on long years of experience in business, financial and economic journalism, apart from other professional fields, although each member’s record of coverage, analysis and commentary would reveal far broader interests. This panel keeps itself in tune with the news as it unfolds and aims to reflect Mint’s views, but cannot claim a daily consensus on every issue of debate that matters. 
As a matter of routine, the Mint Editorial Board produces the newspaper’s Quick Edit, a snappy daily comment on pressing issues, and Our View, a full-length editorial on an issue that demands urgent attention. These are often matters of policy but cover a lot more, as readers may attest. The Board’s mission in expressing opinions, done in the spirit of a "nation in conversation with itself", is aligned with that of Mint: to be "an unbiased and clear-minded chronicler of the Indian Dream".

docs.title: The brain may be about to have its Ozempic moment
docs.text:
Global 
 The brain may be about to have its Ozempic moment
 The Economist , The Economist 7 min read 12 Oct 2026, 06:41 PM IST 
 Summary
 Pharma’s newest obsession involves mimicking the system that keeps people awake 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 ONE PEPTIDE has recently transformed medicine. Drugs based on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut after a meal, began as treatments for diabetes before proving remarkably good at helping people shed weight. They have since shown benefits in the fields of heart disease, kidney disease, sleep apnoea and other ailments. Drugmakers are now betting that two other peptides, the orexins, could follow a similar path for a variety of brain-related ailments.
 Orexins are a pair of neurotransmitters—chemicals that carry messages between neurons. One of the main jobs of these particular neurotransmitters is to regulate wakefulness. And a new generation of drugs designed to mimic their effects is approaching the market.
 On August 5th America’s drug regulator approved oveporexton, made by Takeda, a Japanese pharmaceutical firm, as the first orexin agonist (ie, molecule that stimulates the same cell-surface receptors) for narcolepsy, a disorder that leaves patients excessively sleepy by day and prone to nod off without warning. Alkermes, an Irish biotech, is developing a competitor. Eli Lilly, whose fortunes GLP-1s have transformed, does not intend to miss another peptide boom. In June it bought Centessa, a biotech with an orexin drug in early trials, in a deal worth up to $7.8bn, depending on the trials’ success. Morgan Stanley, a bank, reckons orexin medicines could generate $16bn a year by 2035 from narcolepsy and related sleep disorders alone. The current crop of narcolepsy drugs, by contrast, have annual sales of some $3bn.
 And the excitement is not just about narcolepsy, which is estimated to afflict one person in 2,000 in America. Orexins help co-ordinate sleep, attention, motivation and the brain’s reward system. Drugmakers hope orexin medicines could eventually treat depression, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and addiction, conditions that burden hundreds of millions of people.
 Orexins were discovered nearly three decades ago by two teams working independently. In January 1998 Luis de Lecea and his colleagues at the Scripps Research Institute in La Jolla, California found the peptides and called them hypocretins. Weeks later a group led by Yanagisawa Masashi, of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Centre in Dallas, reported that injecting the same peptides into rats’ brains made the animals eat more. They named the molecules orexins, from the Greek orexis, meaning appetite.
 Orexins’ true role emerged the following year. Emmanuel Mignot, of Stanford University, was studying hereditary narcolepsy in Doberman pinschers and Labrador retrievers, dog breeds prone to sudden collapse mid-play. He showed that a mutation blocked the brain’s ability to respond to them. That same year, Dr Yanagisawa’s laboratory found that mice engineered to lack orexins repeatedly fell asleep and collapsed. Human confirmation followed: narcoleptic patients had lost the specialised neurons that produce orexins.
 These neurons inhabit the hypothalamus, a brain region tucked behind the eyes. Once released, orexins lock, depending on their nature, onto one of two types of cell-surface receptors, OX1R and OX2R, in neighbouring neurons, switching them on. It is OX2R that is important for maintaining wakefulness. Its activation stimulates several wakefulness-promoting systems that rely on other neurotransmitters—norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamine and so on—and keeps them working together, rather like the conductor of an orchestra. OX1R, is more involved with reward and motivation.
 You are feeling sleepy...
 Drugmakers first learned how to turn the OX2R conductor off. Orexin antagonists (which block the molecules’ actions rather than mimicking them, and thus promote sleep), have been available since 2014 as treatments for insomnia. They work differently from conventional sleeping pills, which enhance GABA, one of the brain’s main inhibitory neurotransmitters.
 Birgitte Kornum, an orexins expert at Copenhagen University, says such pills induce sedation rather than natural sleep and often lose efficacy with continued use. Orexin antagonists instead turn down the brain’s wakefulness signal, letting its sleep-promoting systems take over.
 The bigger prize may lie not in blocking orexin’s signal, but restoring it—for many sleep disorders stem from faulty orexin signalling. The immediate application people have in mind is for narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), in which excessive daytime sleepiness is accompanied by cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle control typically triggered by strong emotion. Further down the line narcolepsy type 2 (NT2), which lacks cataplexy, and idiopathic hypersomnia, a related type of excessive daytime sleepiness, are also in drugmakers’ crosshairs.
 NT1 is caused by abnormally low levels of the orexin that binds to OX2R. During REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, the phase when dreams are most intense, the brain paralyses the body to stop it actually acting out movements involved in such dreams. When someone is awake, this paralysis is held in check by norepinephrine and serotonin—two neurotransmitters that orexin sustains. With insufficient orexin, the paralysis circuit may fire even if a person is fully conscious. They might be wide awake, in the middle of a burst of laughter for example, and then lose muscle control and crumple to the floor.
 Turning orexins back on is, however, harder than switching them off. An antagonist need only fit into a receptor to prevent an orexin from binding. An agonist must actually reproduce the effect of a peptide many times the drug’s own size. It must also cross the blood-bra

docs.title: China’s weakening economy is creating a lost generation
docs.text:
Global 
 China’s weakening economy is creating a lost generation
 Hannah Miao , The Wall Street Journal 12 min read 13 Oct 2026, 06:46 AM IST 
 Summary
 Young people are watching their bright futures disappear as the country’s job losses pile up and the milestones of adulthood slip further away. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DALI, China—For months, Ma Yongjian didn’t tell his parents where he was.
 Halfway through a master’s degree in computer science, the 27-year-old stopped going to class last year. Software engineering used to be a safe career choice, but the rise of artificial intelligence and a wave of layoffs at Chinese tech companies left Ma convinced he wouldn’t be able to land a good job. He no longer saw the point of studying.
 When his roommates left their dorm each morning, Ma would wander Beijing, sitting in parks and looking at stray cats. Earlier this year, he escaped to Dali, a magnet for drifters in China’s Yunnan province known for its scenic mountains and slow pace of life.
 His parents thought he was still in grad school. He didn’t want to worry them.
 “Before, everyone expected life would keep getting better, your income would keep growing. Now, it’s different,” said Ma. “When you look at the future, there isn’t much hope.”
 A generation born during China’s boom years is now entering adulthood with dwindling opportunities , fiercer competition and a growing sense of despondency that years of hard work have left them no better off than their parents—and, for some, back living with them. Steady jobs are hard to get, pushing millions into the precarious gig economy, while others buckle under a cutthroat work culture.
 A weakened economy has shrunk the job market, just as record numbers of college graduates are looking to start their careers. The rapid adoption of AI is adding to the uncertainty.
 Many top employers, including tech giants Alibaba and ByteDance, have been quietly cutting staff. Although the companies aren’t publicly blaming AI, the technology has been a factor, people familiar with the matter say. Other industries, from filmmaking to finance, are using AI to scale back hiring.
 Beijing has gone all in on the technology, urging companies to rapidly embrace AI to make the economy more competitive. But there are signs officials are also growing concerned about the impact on social stability. They’ve warned employers not to cut jobs as they adopt AI, people familiar with the matter say.
 The warnings came after Vice Premier He Lifeng polled China’s biggest employers last year, and some estimated AI could wipe out 30% or more of their existing roles, the people said. He seemed shaken by the responses, one said.
 As job losses pile up, the typical milestones of adulthood—financial independence, a stable career, marriage, parenthood—are feeling out of reach for much of Gen Z.
 The urban jobless rate among 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, stands at roughly 19% as of August, compared with about 9% among the same age group in the U.S. It’s 7.5% for those aged 25 to 29, compared with 5.3% in the U.S., and above China’s overall unemployment rate of around 5%. Wage growth has stagnated.
 For now, the mood is more resignation than anger, especially with many parents pitching in to help with living costs. But there’s a risk young people’s disillusionment could harden into something more dangerous for the Communist Party, like unrest.
 It could also have broader implications for China’s future.
 Struggling to start
 Faced with an uncertain outlook, young people are delaying marriage. The birthrate has plummeted. Some Gen Z are simply checking out, living off savings. Earlier this year, the country’s intelligence agency warned young people to resist “lying flat,” a buzzword for doing the bare minimum.
 Zhang Tian, 27, said her mother wants her to have a stable job, get married and have children. But she and her boyfriend of five years are nowhere near thinking of settling down. They’re struggling just to get careers off the ground.
 Zhang’s parents, born in the 1970s, didn’t go to university and were assigned government-related jobs that they still have. Eager to do something more creative, Zhang studied landscape architecture. It seemed smart given China’s booming real-estate market.
 Around the time she graduated in 2021, the property bubble burst.
 About six months into her first job at a real-estate developer in Hangzhou, she was laid off. She eventually landed a role in Shanghai as an administrative assistant, but her salary—roughly $1,200 a month—was lower than before. Late last year, she lost her job again.
 “Dating and being in a relationship is an emotional matter, but getting married and having kids is a financial one,” said Zhang, who is from Jiangsu province north of Shanghai. “I don’t think we’ve sorted out our financial situation yet, so we aren’t considering getting married yet.”
 She and her boyfriend, Cheng Ming, plan to study AI in hopes of finding tech jobs. But that sector is unstable, too.
 Cheng, after getting laid off from two real-estate firms, started taking online classes to learn about software. He landed a role in sales at a small tech company—only to see the firm go bankrupt. He was laid off yet again in April.
 “Inside, there’s a feeling of being weighed down by society,” Cheng said, “a sense of resignation.”
 ‘Fairly bleak’
 The central problem is that China isn’t creating enough stable, high-paying jobs.
 Overall economic growth has been weak in recent years, expanding at a significantly slower pace than before the pandemic. Although a few industries favored by Beijing, such as robotics, are booming, their labor needs are limited. Many young people don’t want to toil in factories, which don’t provide the kind of prestige or work environments college graduates seek—and are rapidly replacing workers with robots.

Nifty weekly expiry in focus; Analysts decode charts, derivatives positions
 Based on the options data, on Tuesday the focus will be on the 22,250-22,500 range owing to Nifty's weekly expiry, says Dharmesh Bhatt, Head-Derivatives Research at Systematix Institutional.
 Nifty Tuesday expiry: Dharmesh Bhatt of Systematix Institutional expects Nifty to move in the 22,250-22,500 range. (File Photo)
 Rex Cano Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 8:13 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion. The NSE Nifty 50 index plunged almost 350 points or 1.5 per cent in Monday's intraday deals, before settling with a loss of 0.7 per cent or 157 points at 22,363. In doing so, analysts suggest the Nifty may have lost the momentum it regained on Friday. This morning, GIFT Nifty indicated a likely quiet start to the trading action as high crude oil prices continue to weigh on market sentiment. That apart, the weekly Nifty options expiry could sway the market mood either way. Dharmesh Bhatt, Head-Derivatives Research at Systematix Institutional Research says that the Nifty's recovery has lost momentum, with the index giving back ground after Friday's sharp rally and returning to the support zone. The analyst flags that the base-building thesis remains intact only while 21,900 holds, but rising volatility and renewed deterioration in derivatives positioning keep the broader trend bearish. Bhatt adds that the volume was the lowest in three weeks, indicating limited participation and a lack of conviction behind the move. From the weekly options expiry perspective Bhatt says the focus will be on the 22,250–22,500 range, with 22,371 as the first downside test and 22,300 and 22,000 as put-support levels. CHECK Stock Market LIVE Updates "The 22,500 strike remains a heavy positioning zone on both sides. With spot below the flip, sharp moves remain possible," the analyst explains. Meanwhile, Om Mehra, Technical Research Analyst at SAMCO Securities notes that fresh Call writing was concentrated between the 22,400 and 22,600 strikes, with the heaviest addition at 22,600, creating a strong overhead resistance zone. On the Put side, meaningful unwinding was seen at 22,500, suggesting that some nearby support was withdrawn. The Put Call Ratio (PCR) stands at 0.67, reflecting clear Call side dominance, says Mehra. Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, Founder & CEO of HST Wealth reckons that the Nifty on Tuesday must defend the 22,300–22,200 zone and reclaim 22,500–22,600 for the mildly positive opening to become a meaningful rebound. "Failure to sustain the opening strength could bring 22,200 and eventually 22,000 back into focus," cautions Radhakrishnan. Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money flags that the Nifty is trading below its key moving averages, indicating that the broader technical structure remains weak and selling pressure continues to dominate. The analyst sees 22,400–22,500 as the immediate resistance zone, and as the crucial hurdle that the Nifty needs to break decisively. On the downside, Ponmudi sees near support at 22,300, followed by the crucial 22,180–22,200 zone. As a broader market trend perspective, Nandish Shah, Deputy Vice President at HDFC Securities says that the short-term trend remains bearish, with the Nifty trading below its 11- and 20-day Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs). Shah believes that a sustained move above last week's high of 22,776 would be needed to signal a bullish trend reversal. "On the downside, 22,180 is the near-term support; a break below this level could signal a resumption of the downtrend," Shah adds.

Equity mutual fund inflows hit 5-month high on small, midcap rush
 Investors used mkt correction to raise equity bets, average cost, say experts
 Active mutual funds are sector-agnostic and those manage a portfolio of securities (Representative Image)
 Abhishek Kumar Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 7:08 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Net inflows into schemes of active equity mutual funds (MFs) rose 31 per cent in September over August, reaching a five-month high of ₹38,307 crore, as investors continued to ramp up allocation to midcap and smallcap funds. 
 The two categories, which have seen their combined net inflows increase in each of the past four months, attracted a record ₹15,740 crore in September, up 5 per cent over August. 
 “They accounted for approximately 44 per cent of net equity inflows in September. The sustained interest in these categories, despite the correction in the broader markets, suggests that investors continue to remain confident about the long-term growth potential of emerging businesses,” said Himanshu Srivastava, principal, manager research, Morningstar Investment Research India. 
 Market correction in September came after a rally in mid and smallcap stocks in the previous months. The Nifty Midcap 100 declined 7.6 per cent while the Nifty Smallcap 250 fell 3.1 per cent. 
 They had logged gains in each of the previous five months, leading to their outperformance over largecap indices, which have struggled since the start of the United States-Iran conflict at the end of February.

 “Investors seemed to have taken market drawdown as an opportunity to add to their portfolio and average their acquisition costs,” said Manish Mehta, chief business officer, SBI Mutual Fund. 
 Inflows strengthened across other categories as well. Flexicap funds recorded a 32 per cent month-on-month increase in net inflows to ₹6,702 crore, while largecap funds rang up ₹860 crore after witnessing net outflows of over ₹1,000 crore in each of the previous two months. 
 “The return of positive inflows into largecap funds is encouraging particularly because valuations have become relatively attractive, providing a favourable outlook for the category in the future,” said Saugata Chatterjee, president and deputy chief executive officer, Nippon India Mutual Fund. 
 The overall increase in net inflows into active equity schemes came as gross investment in active equity schemes rose to a six-month high, while redemptions moderated for a second consecutive month to their lowest level in four months. 
 Net inflows stood at ₹29,329 crore in August. 
 Inflows were supported by systematic investment plans (SIPs), the investment in which rose by nearly ₹200 crore to a new high of ₹32,490 crore, shows the data released by the Association of Mutual Funds in India (Amfi). 
 “This reflects continued investor participation in systematic investing,” said Venkat Chalasani, chief executive, Amfi. 
 However, debt funds recorded a net outflow of ₹1.8 trillion, largely driven by quarter-end withdrawal from liquid and other short-duration funds to meet advance tax payments and other liquidity requirements. The outflows, along with the mark-to-market losses, resulted in a 5 per cent month-on-month decline in assets under management to ₹87 trillion.

DMart's margin recovery may take time amid rising costs, store expansion
 Despite strong revenue growth and improving same-store sales, DMart faces margin pressure from rising costs, store expansion and competition, delaying profitability gains
 premium 
 DMart issued 111 million bills during the quarter, implying Y-o-Y growth of 14.4 per cent (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 11:14 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 The Q2FY27 Avenue Supermarts (DMart) performance was lower than expected. Revenue growth was 18.4 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y). But margin pressure was visible.
 Gross margin declined 10 basis points (bps) Y-o-Y to 14.1 per cent, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margin contracted 28 bps Y-o-Y to 7.3 per cent.
 Adjusted net profit grew 7.6 per cent to ₹804 crore, with net profit margin down 42 bps to 4.2 per cent.
 Reacting to this, the stock shed 4.5 per cent to ₹3,362 and was the top loser in BSE 100 on Monday.
 Same-store sales growth (SSSG) for stores operational for two years or more improved to 9.5 per cent in Q2FY27 (6.8 per cent in Q2FY26). But lower-margin sales, operating cost pressures and store expansion have put a ceiling on profits.
 Revenue per square feet declined 0.9 per cent to ₹8,975, while Ebitda per square feet fell 4.6 per cent to ₹656. Revenue per store declined 1.2 per cent to ₹37.1 crore, while Ebitda per store contracted 4.9 per cent to ₹2.7 crore. The expanding store network should gradually become more profitable.
 During Q2FY27, food revenue grew 19.2 per cent, while non-foods and general merchandise & apparel (GM&A) revenue increased 16.8 per cent and 17.8 per cent, respectively. Food carries lower margins than other categories and it contributes 59 per cent to revenue. Employee costs increased 2 bps as a percentage of revenue. Other expenses rose 16 bps Y-o-Y.
 DMart issued 111 million bills during the quarter, implying Y-o-Y growth of 14.4 per cent. The company added 15 stores (18 stores in H1FY27), taking the store count to 518. The company added 85 stores in FY26 compared with 50 in FY25. DMart has a target of 15 per cent annual store-count expansion. The management highlighted that legacy stores in markets like Mumbai and Bengaluru have reached maturity reducing upside from like-for-like growth. Intensifying competition from quick-commerce and e-commerce players will also be a factor.
 DMart Ready is focused on improving the operating model and deepening presence in large markets.
 The online business was operational in 19 cities a year ago and it has reduced to 11 cities as part of the change in operating model. The online segment is a new channel but profitability is going to be driven by unit economics and scale. In Q3FY27, results could be boosted by a lower base in Q3FY26 (13.2 per cent Y-o-Y), the goods and services tax (GST) transition impact, and movement in festival timings.
 The capex in FY26 was ₹4,100 crore and capex through the next three financial years would be closer to ₹5,000 crore per year.
 Capex is up 22 per cent Y-o-Y. Employee expenses increased 20 per cent. There is an 87 per cent rise in interest costs and a 29 per cent decline in other income, reflecting higher borrowings. 
 Given the ongoing expansion, and the product mix with its high share of food, operating leverage should improve gradually.
 This implies Ebitda margins would be around 7.5 per cent for FY27 and move up by around 20 bps in the next two financial years.
 As stores mature, the revenue per sq feet should improve by mid-single digits.
 Revenue, Ebitda and net profit annual growth should be high teens until FY29.
 One positive is good working capital management, with the inventory cycle at 38-40 days and net working capital cycle at 28 days. But due to the expansion, there has been an inventory build-up and working capital has risen to ₹1,900 crore from ₹700 crore a year ago. Net debt (ex-lease) surged to ₹2,500 crore against ₹700 crore in March 2026.
 Consolidated revenue grew 18 per cent Y-o-Y to Rs 19,640 crore, and consolidated EBITDA rose 15 per cent Y-o-Y to Rs 1,390 crore as the Ebitda margin dipped 20 bps to 7.1 per cent. Operating losses at subsidiaries dropped to 2.3 per cent (3.6 per cent Y-o-Y and 6.1 per cent quarter-on-quarter or Q-o-Q). Consolidated net profit grew 8 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹740 crore and consolidated net profit margin contracted 35 bps to 3.8 per cent. The trend towards lower margins and higher costs allied with higher competitive intensity, is likely to disappoint investors.
 Analysts have cut earnings estimates as it seems growth in revenue will take a while to translate into higher profitability. The writer is a New Delhi-based independent journalist

docs.title: 3 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Jefferies with 28% to 50% upside
docs.text: Global investment bank Jefferies has identified opportunities across these themes, assigning ‘Buy’ ratings to three stocks with potential upside ranging from 28% to 50% from their respective market prices. Jefferies picks are Can Fin Homes, Adani Green Energy and Poonawalla Fincorp. While the housing finance lender faces questions over loan growth, the renewable energy company could benefit from rising power demand. Poonawalla Fincorp, meanwhile, is banking on its expanding loan portfolio and improving margins. Let's take a look at the key reasons behind the bullish call - Jefferies on Can Fin Homes: 50% upside potential Jefferies has assigned a ‘Buy’ rating to Can Fin Homes, with a target price of Rs 1,075, indicating an upside potential of 50%. The company reported a 9% year-on-year (YoY) increase in September-quarter profit after tax (PAT) to Rs 275 crore. This was 3% above Jefferies’ estimate, supported by lower provisions and operating expenses. However, loan growth showed signs of moderation. Assets under management (AUM), which represent the total outstanding loans managed by the company, grew 10%, compared with 11% in the previous quarter. Disbursements declined 7% year-on-year as technology implementation disrupted operations. ALSO READWhere to invest Rs 10 lakh now: 5 top Fund Managers reveal the ultimate ‘Model Portfolio’ According to the report, “AUM growth moderated to 10% (11% June Q) as disbursements (-7% YoY) was impacted by tech implementation driven disruption.” Jefferies also noted that funding costs and credit provisions would remain relevant to the company’s performance. Jefferies on Adani Green Energy: 35% upside potential Jefferies has maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on Adani Green Energy and set a target price of Rs 1,695, indicating a 35% upside. Its report noted that the stock has corrected 22% from its peak and trades at 20 times one-year forward enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EV/EBITDA). Jefferies expects earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 30% between FY26-30. The global investment believes stronger electricity demand, higher temperatures and improved utilisation could support growth. It also sees potential demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS), with the company planning to expand capacity beyond 10 gigawatt-hours by the end of FY2027. According to the report, “We continue see risk-reward as attractive and retain our 'Buy' rating.” However, execution delays, particularly at Khavda, and aggressive bidding remain key risks. Jefferies on Poonawalla Fincorp: 28% upside potential Poonawalla Fincorp offers another opportunity in the financial services sector, with Jefferies setting a target price of Rs 560, implying a 28% upside. The company’s September-quarter PAT rose 22% sequentially to Rs 370 crore, exceeding the brokerage’s estimate by 4%. Its AUM increased 55% year-on-year to Rs 74,000 crore, supported by growth in lending. ALSO READ2 Electrolyser stocks in India’s Rs 19,744-cr green hydrogen race—Who has the edge? Jefferies expects newer loan products to drive further expansion. It forecasts AUM to grow at a 40% CAGR over FY2026-FY2028. Improving lending yields and lower credit costs could also support profitability. The brokerage highlighted that “New product scale up should drive 40% AUM CAGR over FY27-28e.” Asset quality showed improvement during the quarter, with gross stage-three assets (GS3), a measure of seriously stressed loans, declining to 1.2%. Credit costs also fell sequentially. What should investors watch? For Can Fin Homes, the loan disbursements need to recover. Adani Green Energy depends partly on capacity expansion and electricity demand, while Poonawalla Fincorp’s outlook rests on loan growth and improving profitability. docs.title: Suzlon share price down 31% in 3 months: Why Motilal Oswal sees 73% upside potential
docs.text: This renewable stock has fallen 31% in three months But the domestic brokerage house Motilal Oswal, in its report dated October 11, sees an upside potential of 73% for the stock. Motilal Oswal has kept its 'Buy' rating on Suzlon Energy, the wind turbine maker, with a target price of Rs 65. This implies 73% upside from current levels. According to the brokerage report, the key factors fuelling the bullish call are a large order book, an expected recovery in deliveries and rising demand for wind power as India’s electricity needs increase. Let's take a look at the key reasons why the brokerage house is bullish on this stock and the rationale behind it - Suzlon: A 5.9 GW order book offers delivery visibility For a wind turbine manufacturer, a strong order book matters because it provides a clearer picture of future business. Suzlon’s order book stood at 5.9 gigawatts (GW) at the end of the Q1FY27. The company also received around 1.3 GW of orders during the financial year so far. According to Motilal Oswal, this provides full visibility on its estimated deliveries through the third quarter of FY28. The brokerage expects Suzlon’s deliveries to increase by 35% year-on-year to 3.3 GW in FY27, including 2.1 GW in the second half. Deliveries are estimated to rise further to 3.8 GW in FY28. ALSO READFrom no dividend to 3.5% yield: This PSU bank’s profit-led comeback is not over The brokerage noted that it typically accounts for 60-65% of Suzlon’s annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA). Motilal Oswal expects EBITDA to grow at a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 22% between FY26 and FY28. Suzlon: Wind power demand could create room for growth The second factor is the wider market for wind energy. India added around 3 GW of wind capacity in the first half of FY27, according to the report. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) expects additions of 7.5-8 GW for the full financial year. Historically, second-half installations have been around 1.5 times those in the first half, the brokerage noted. Rising electricity demand could also support wind power. India recorded peak power demand of 269 gigawatts on September 10, 2026. Demand during evening hours is particularly relevant because solar generation declines after sunset. According to Motilal Oswal, this could support wind-solar hybrid projects and Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) projects, which aim to supply renewable electricity according to a specified schedule. The report also pointed to rising evening power prices. Average May evening peak prices increased from Rs 8.08 per kilowatt-hour in 2023 to Rs 9.71 in 2026, according to figures cited from the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM) paper. Suzlon: New opportunities beyond turbine deliveries Motilal Oswal identifies three additional opportunities. This includes repowering older wind farms, exports and its development company (DevCo) model. Repowering involves replacing or upgrading older wind turbines to improve their output. The brokerage estimates that India could have up to 25 GW of repowering opportunities, as a large part of the existing wind fleet was commissioned 10-20 years ago. Suzlon is also evaluating export opportunities in Europe, Australia, Latin America and Southeast Asia. Meanwhile, its DevCo model had secured more than 600 megawatts (MW) of orders within the first four months of FY27, accounting for 60% of total orders, the report said. ALSO READWhy Rs 38,800 crore monthly Mutual Fund inflows fail to lift Nifty: Jefferies explains What investors need to watch Apart from growth opportunities, execution remains important. Suzlon will need to convert its order book into deliveries and achieve the expected improvement in profitability. Suzlon’s stock was trading at 17.5 times estimated FY28 earnings after its recent correction, around 20% below its one-year forward mean minus one standard deviation valuation level of 22 times, according to the report. docs.title: Poonawalla Fincorp up 8% on Q2 profit surge; Jefferies, Motilal see 23% upside potential
docs.text: The Poonawalla Fincorp is buzzing in trade today, October 12, after the non-banking financial company’s (NBFC) net profit for the second quarter of financial year 2027 (Q2FY27) surged over five times year-on-year. The share price of Poonawalla Fincorp soared over 8% in early trade today, before giving up some of the gains. Its net profit for Q2FY27 jumped over five times year-on-year to Rs 374.85 crore. Its total revenue from operations rose 70% to Rs 2,624.84 crore. Global investment bank Jefferies has retained its ‘Buy’ recommendation on the stock and has a price target of Rs 560 apiece. This implies an upside of nearly 21% from the stock’s current price of Rs 462.90 apiece. Domestic brokerage house Motilal Oswal maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock while brokerage Emkay Global retained its ‘Reduce’ recommendation. Brokerage JM Financial upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Add’. ALSO READTitan’s smaller rivals match its growth—at 41%–85% P/E discounts Jefferies on Poonawalla Fincorp: New products to drive growth The NBFC’s profit growth for the quarter was led by better net interest margins (NIM). The growth in its assets under management (AUM) also continued, rising 55% YoY, led by growth in disbursements. Jefferies has projected a 40% growth in AUM on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) basis over FY26 to FY28. This growth will be driven by strategic reset and as new products scale. Jefferies has raised its FY27 and FY28 estimated earnings per share (EPS) view by 8% and 6%, respectively, as stronger growth, higher NIMs, and lower credit cost estimates more than offset lower fee income estimates. The proposed commission caps by IRDAI remain a risk to Poonawalla Fincorp’s fee income. “We expect credit cost to decline over FY26–29E (2.7% in FY26) due to fading legacy stress, lower new slippages and portfolio mix,” Jefferies said, adding that strong growth and ROE expansion can support premium valuations. Motiall Oswal on Poonawalla Fincorp: Strong momentum Motilal Oswal has maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and has a target price of Rs 570 apiece. This implies an upside of 23% from the current price. The brokerage has also raised its FY27 and FY28 EPS estimates by 3% each, to factor in slightly higher NIM. “Poonawalla Fincorp remains disciplined in its growth approach, with management highlighting strong business momentum across newer product segments. Disbursements continue to gain traction sequentially, supported by an expanding presence and a wider distribution network. We expect PFL to deliver an AUM CAGR of 44% over FY26-28E,” it said. Motilal Oswal expects NIM to expand 7.7% in FY27, and 7.9% in FY28, including the benefit of primary equity capital raised at the beginning of FY27. Emkay Global on Poonawalla Fincorp: AI-led productivity Emkay Global retained its ‘Reduce’ rating on the stock and has a price target of Rs 410 apiece. This implies a downside of 11% from the stock’s current price. “The management expects strong growth momentum to continue, targeting a 35–40% AUM CAGR over the medium term, driven by scaling new businesses, aggressive gold loan branch expansion, and deeper digital cross-selling. The focus remains firmly on structural, predictable profitability, which is expected to be supported by margin expansion led by strong pricing power, with incremental disbursement yields ~200bps higher than the portfolio yield,” the brokerage said. “Operating leverage is projected to build over the next two years, balancing front-loaded opex with significant AI-driven productivity gains (84 live enterprise AI projects that are actively lowering acquisition costs and enhancing operational efficiency). Finally, on asset quality, the management expects credit costs to improve, attributing the portfolio’s resilience to rigorous, AI-backed cohort calibration, and superior early-vintage performance,” it added. JM Financial on Poonawalla Fincorp: Attractive entry point Brokerage JM Financial has upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Add’ and has raised its target price by 4% to Rs 550. This implies an upside of nearly 19%. “Stock price has corrected 5–9% over the last one–two months leading to correction in current valuation to 2.2x of FY28E. The current multiple largely captures the growth opportunity, but it does not adequately reflect the potential improvement in return ratios and franchise quality, offering an attractive entry point,” JM Financial said. ALSO READWhy Rs 38,800 crore monthly Mutual Fund inflows fail to lift Nifty: Jefferies explains “Factoring in margin expansion, improving operating efficiency and moderating credit costs, we are raising FY27/28 EPS estimates by ~3%/4% and increasing target price by 4% to INR 550 (from INR 530), valuing the stock at 2.7x FY28E BVPS,” it said. Poonawalla Fincorp: What next for investors Most brokerage reports indicate that the current earnings performance captures the growth opportunity. However, the street is awaiting potential improvement in return ratios and franchise quality and many analysts see the current levels as a good entry point for the stock. docs.title: Why Rs 38,800 crore monthly Mutual Fund inflows fail to lift Nifty: Jefferies explains
docs.text: The Indian equity benchmarks have significantly underperformed their global peers this year. The market continues to be bogged down by high crude oil prices, elevated US bond yields, and persistent selling by foreign investors. The monthly net inflows into domestic equity have averaged Rs 38,800 crore or $4.1 billion so far this year, according to global investment bank Jefferies. However, the inflows continue to be absorbed by equity issuances that have picked up again in recent months. Domestic fund flows: Tracking the trend Jefferies said monthly equity supply declined from a peak of $10.4 billion in June 2025 to $1 billion in April 2026, following the outbreak of the West Asia war. However, this has subsequently rebounded to $9.5 billion in August. ALSO READ2 Electrolyser stocks in India’s Rs 19,744-cr green hydrogen race—Who has the edge? “This supply dynamic is having the practical impact of limiting the upside of the benchmark Nifty Index,” the global investment bank said. The smaller stocks have continued to outperform the big caps this year in spite of higher valuations. “From a stock market standpoint, the mid and small cap segment has been the most interesting part of the equity market,” it said. “The Nifty MidCap 100 Index is trading on 22.9x 12-month forward earnings, compared with 17.0x for the Nifty. The Nifty Midcap 100 Index has declined by 1.9% year-to-date and is up 88% since the start of 2023, while the Nifty is down 13.4% year-to-date and up 25% since the beginning of 2023. As a result, the top 20 stocks account for a declining percentage of India’s total stock market capitalisation, falling from 44% to 27% since 2020. This is the complete opposite of the trend globally given the surge in passive investing,” Jefferies added. Till September, India’s primary market recorded as many as 82 IPOs. Some of the biggest IPOs so far this year include marquee names like the National Stock Exchange, SBI Funds Management, and Manipal Health Enterprises. Jefferies on India: Betting on cyclical rebound According to Jefferies, “the structural growth story (for India) remains intact with the economic data remarkably resilient given the obvious challenges posed by geopolitics to a country which remains a major consumer of energy.” Jefferies had maintained India as a slight Overweight last quarter on signs of a cyclical rebound in domestic demand. India has outperformed the Asia Pacific benchmark, excluding Japan, by 17% since April 2020. “However, valuations are still at a premium to the rest of the region,” Jefferies said. “India again underperformed last quarter, declining by 5.9% in US dollar terms. It is also an underperformer year to date declining by 15.6%, a performance which incorporates a further 6.2% depreciation of the rupee against the US dollar year to date after a 4.7% depreciation last year,” it added. ALSO READBrokerage consensus stock picks: 3 ‘Buy’ rated stocks with 19% to 70% upside potential Jefferies forecasts 17% earnings growth The view of Jefferies’ India office is that the nominal GDP acceleration should lead to a pickup in earnings growth from 14% this fiscal year to 17% next fiscal year. The 10-year Treasury bond yield remains the most important price in world financial markets. Jefferies believes “the arrival of a new Fed chair has increased the importance of the American central bank.” They are betting on Kevin Warsh’s stated commitment at the September FOMC meeting “to hit the 2% inflation target when inflation has now been above that target in the US for more than five years.”

docs.title: 2 Electrolyser stocks in India’s Rs 19,744-cr green hydrogen race—Who has the edge?
docs.text: Green hydrogen, produced by splitting water through electrolysis using renewable electricity, is emerging as a potential industrial fuel for fertiliser, oil refining, steelmaking and shipping. According to Grand View Research, the global green hydrogen market is estimated at US$1.7 billion in 2026, up from US$1.1 billion in 2025, and is projected to reach US$11.7 billion by 2033, implying a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 32.2%. India’s opportunity is driven by its National Green Hydrogen Mission, approved with an outlay of ₹19,744 crore, including ₹17,490 crore for incentives covering electrolyser manufacturing and hydrogen production. The mission targets 5 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of green hydrogen production by 2030, supported by approximately 125 gigawatts (GW) of additional renewable energy capacity and more than ₹8 lakh crore in expected investment. By March 2026, the government had awarded 3 GW per annum of electrolyser manufacturing capacity to 15 companies and 8.62 MTPA of green hydrogen production capacity to 18 companies. However, only around 8,000 TPA of production capacity had been commissioned by February 2026. This gap between planned capacity and operating projects raises a crucial question for manufacturers such as L&T and Thermax: which electrolyser factories can secure real demand before capital costs mount? FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Larsen & Toubro: Can India’s Engineering Giant Turn Electrolysers Into a Profitable Business? Larsen & Toubro (L&T) is an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) company with businesses spanning infrastructure, energy, manufacturing, defence and technology. Its green energy operations combine electrolyser manufacturing with the development and execution of hydrogen and derivative projects. Through L&T Electrolysers Limited, it manufactures high-pressure alkaline electrolysers at Hazira, Gujarat, while L&T Energy GreenTech develops green hydrogen projects. This combination gives L&T two potential revenue streams: supplying equipment and engineering systems, and developing projects that produce and sell hydrogen. Hazira’s Manufacturing Edge Needs Commercial Proof L&T’s Hazira facility is India’s first giga-scale expandable high-pressure alkaline electrolyser manufacturing facility. The company has indigenised more than 85% of its electrolyser supply chain and developed a 4 MW electrolyser stack using zero-gap technology. Its in-house research and development and testing facilities support further product development. These given capabilities can improve supply security and lower reliance on imported components. However, localisation alone does not establish cost competitiveness. Readers still need evidence of manufacturing utilisation, equipment deliveries, realised selling prices, warranty costs and margins. L&T has not separately disclosed electrolyser revenue or manufacturing profitability in its financial reporting. Panipat Provides a Demand Anchor, but Project Returns Remain Unclear L&T Energy GreenTech has secured a project with Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) to supply 10,000 tonnes of green hydrogen annually to the Panipat refinery for 25 years. The project uses alkaline electrolysers manufactured at Hazira. L&T has also commissioned a 1 MW green hydrogen plant for Deendayal Port Authority at Kandla, Gujarat. The commercial distinction between equipment supply and hydrogen production is crucial. Equipment sales can generate revenue as products are delivered, whereas a build-own-operate project requires capital investment before recurring hydrogen sales begin. Its financial performance depends on construction costs, financing, renewable electricity prices, operating efficiency, maintenance and the agreed selling price of hydrogen. The government’s own hydrogen procurement data illustrates the cost challenge. Competitive bidding under the National Green Hydrogen Mission discovered prices of ₹397 per kilogram, including goods and services tax (GST), for supply to IOCL’s refinery and ₹387 per kilogram for refineries operated by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited. These are procurement prices, not evidence of L&T’s realised selling price or project margin. The Manufacturing Segment Cannot Stand in for Hydrogen Earnings L&T’s Manufacturing & Products segment reported revenue of ₹4,648 crore in Q1FY27, up 8.7% year-on-year from ₹4,276 crore in Q1FY26. Segment profit declined to ₹593 crore from ₹646 crore. The segment includes precision engineering, heavy engineering, defence electronics and other businesses, so neither its revenue nor its profit can be attributed solely to electrolysers. Consolidated revenue from operations rose 6.7% year-on-year to ₹67,942 crore in Q1FY27, while consolidated profit after tax (PAT), including joint ventures and associates, increased 15.5% to ₹4,988 crore. Both figures declined sequentially from Q4FY26. Operating cash flow, excluding Financial Services, stood at ₹4,300 crore during the quarter, against group collections of ₹65,800 crore on the same exclusion basis. The consolidated debt-equity ratio was 1.01 at June 2026, or 1.12 including borrowings classified as held for sale. These figures demonstrate the scale of L&T’s wider operations and provide context for its funding capacity. But because L&T does not publish separate financials for its electrolyser business, it does not show how much capital the hydrogen business requires or whether it generates positive cash flow. Does the Valuation Allow Room for Execution Risk? Source: Screener.in; Stock Price as on 8th October 2026 L&T’s share price declined approximately 6% over six months and 1% over one year. Its price-to-earnings (PE) ratio stood at 28.9. On 7 October 2026, Motilal Oswal Financial Services maintained a Buy rating with a target price of ₹4,400.

docs.title: From no dividend to 3.5% yield: This PSU bank’s profit-led comeback is not over
docs.text: Welcome to the latest edition of Dividend Hunter. In recent weeks, we have analysed companies where strong cash flows could translate into consistent dividends. In our previous edition, we covered a public sector undertaking (PSU) Bank that delivered a 3.7% dividend yield. This week, in our 'Dividend Hunter' series, we are discussing another fast-growing and India’s sixth-largest government-owned bank with a market capitalisation of ₹1,08,476 crore as of October 9, 2026. In FY26, the bank recorded a global business of ₹28.06 lakh crore alongside a record annual net profit of ₹19,187.0 crore. Notably, the bank's revenue grew at a 12% CAGR over the past five years, while net profit rose at a much faster CAGR of 44%. Strong asset quality also supported the company’s profitability. Gross and Net Non-Performing Asset (NPA) levels were 1.84% and 0.43%, respectively. The bank also delivered a 19.6% return on equity (ROE) and 1.1% return on assets (ROA). The bank maintains a clear policy to deliver periodic cash returns to its shareholders. For FY26, the Board recommended a dividend of ₹4.20 per share. Effectively, this public sector bank continues to balance capital appreciation with shareholder distributions. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now The bank is Canara Bank. Canara Bank Share Price Canara Bank Dividend Track Record: Why Profit Growth Outpaced Payouts Canara Bank paid a per-share dividend of ₹4.20 in FY26, translating into a dividend yield of 3.5% at the current price of ₹120.0. The bank declares a final dividend every June. The bank has increased the per-share payout over the last three financial years, from ₹3.22 in FY24 to ₹4.2 in FY26. Canara Bank split its ₹10 face-value shares into five ₹2 shares each in May 2024. Thus, for better comparison, we have adjusted the post-split dividends to the pre-split basis. On this basis, the dividend per share increased from ₹16.10 in FY24 to ₹20 in FY25 and ₹21 in FY26. This indicates a continued rise in the bank's dividend per share. Historical Comeback: Rebuilding Shareholder Payouts After the Bad Loan Cycle Like the broader PSU Banks, Canara Bank also resumed dividend payments in FY22 after a four-year gap, following a period marked by high NPAs, elevated credit costs and losses. Given the credit growth in the Indian economy and strong asset quality, the bank has reported strong profitability growth. Core Operations: NII Inches Up 0.37% as Margin Contracts 29 bps to 2.51% This growth allowed Canara Bank to pay dividends. In FY26, the bank's total business reached ₹28,06,226 crore, an increase of 12.11% year-on-year. Global deposits grew 9.7% to ₹15,68,678 crore, while global advances grew 15.3% to ₹12,37,548 crore. Because loan growth moved faster than deposit growth, the Credit-Deposit ratio rose to 78.89%, up from 75.07% in FY25. The domestic CASA ratio ended the year FY26 at 29.84%. Total income rose 7.73% year-on-year to ₹1,53,204 crore. Net interest income increased by 0.37% to ₹37,210 crore. Meanwhile, the Net Interest Margin (NIM) decreased to 2.51% from 2.80% in the previous year. NIM fell partially due to a fall in yield on advances. Financials at a Glance Source: Q4FY26 Investor Presentation Over 53% of the bank's loan book is repo-rate linked. As rate cuts transmitted across the portfolio, the yield on advances declined by 54 bps from 8.83% in FY25 to 8.29% in FY26. Further, Canara Bank’s Cost-to-Income ratio rose by 118 bps to 48.45% in FY26 as operating expenses increased. ALSO READMotilal Oswal Mid Cap Fund vs Invesco India Mid Cap Fund: Which is Better? Despite higher expenses, net profit grew by 12.7% to a record ₹19,187 crore. This profitability is key to dividend payout as the Reserve Bank of India guidelines stipulate that dividends must be paid out of current-year net profits. In addition to net earnings, dividend payouts depend directly on asset quality, capital adequacy metrics, and regulatory requirements. Asset Quality Guardrails: Low NPAs Anchor Sustainable Cash Flows As of FY26, Retail, Agriculture, and MSME (RAM) financing expanded to ₹7,30,520 crore, accounting for 59.0% of the domestic loan portfolio. Corporate loans and other advances made up the remaining 41.0%. This mix improved from FY25, when RAM advances held a 58.0% share. Balance Sheet Health: Why PCR at 94.21% Insulates Future Earnings The bank's Gross Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) reached a multi-year low of 1.84% in FY26 (down from 2.94% in FY25), while Net NPAs improved to 0.43% (down from 0.70%). Cash recoveries, tightly contained slippages, disciplined write-offs, and strong portfolio underwriting strengthened asset quality. Strengthening Asset Quality Source: Q4FY26 Investor Presentation This Net NPA ratio is comfortably below the regulatory limit required for dividend declarations. The annual slippage ratio remained well-contained at 0.24% (with total slippages limited to ₹7,030 crore). This highlights disciplined underwriting and fewer additions to non-performing loans. Asset Quality Cushion: High Provisioning Defends Future Balance Sheets A high Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR) of 94.21% (up 151 bps year-on-year) provides a robust buffer against future asset impairment losses (if any). As asset quality strengthened, the annualised credit cost fell by 13 bps to 0.59% in FY26. docs.title: Jio IPO valuation at $107 billion: Why Nomura sees better value in Bharti Airtel
docs.text: India’s biggest phone network is getting ready to list on the stock market. Jio Platforms’ initial public offering (IPO) is close to being launched. The brokerage house Nomura has done the sums. Nomura has examined the potential listing price of Jio Platforms and its implications for the telecom sector. According to reports cited by the brokerage house, Jio Platforms may set its IPO price band at Rs 1,065-1,119 per share. This could value the company at around $101 billion to $107 billion. However, Nomura believes the proposed valuation is below its own estimate, while Bharti Airtel’s telecom business appears cheaper on a comparable earnings basis. Here is what the brokerage report says about the potential IPO, its impact on Reliance Industries and the valuation gap with Bharti Airtel. Let's take a look - Jio IPO valuation: Enterprise value seen around $113-118 billion According to Nomura, the reported price band of Rs 1,065-1,119 per share would value Jio Platforms’ equity at Rs 9.8 lakh crore to Rs 10.3 lakh crore. After adjusting for debt, spectrum-related obligations, lease liabilities and the cash raised through the IPO, its estimated enterprise value (EV) would stand at around $113 billion to $118 billion. ALSO READZetwerk IPO to open on Oct 15: Check price band & grey market trend for Rs 5,012 cr issue Nomura's own enterprise value target for Jio Platforms is around $133 billion, based on 12 times its estimated earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) for June 2028. The reported IPO valuation would therefore be 11% to 15% below the brokerage's estimate. The report estimates that Jio Platforms would trade at 10.5 to 10.9 times its forecast EBITDA for financial year 2028 at the reported price band. Reliance Industries: How could the Jio listing affect its valuation? Reliance Industries holds an estimated 66.4% stake in Jio Platforms. Based on the reported IPO price band, Nomura calculates that this stake could be worth Rs 481-506 per Reliance share before applying a holding company discount. After applying a 20% discount to account for the fact that Reliance owns a stake in a separately valued business, the estimated contribution falls to Rs 385-405 per Reliance share. This is lower than Nomura's existing standalone sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation, which assigns Rs 541 per Reliance share to Jio Platforms. At the upper end of the reported price band, the difference works out to around Rs 136 per Reliance share. The brokerage noted that Reliance shares had already fallen 26% year-to-date, compared with a 14% decline in the Nifty index, as of the report's reference date. It believes the existing share price more than compensates for the potential impact of the lower Jio valuation and holding company discount. Bharti Airtel vs Jio: Which valuation looks cheaper? Nomura's comparison also brings Bharti Airtel into focus. The brokerage estimates that Bharti Airtel's India telecom business trades at 9.2 times its forecast FY2028 EV/EBITDA, compared with 10.5-10.9 times for Jio Platforms. This places Bharti Airtel's implied valuation at a discount of around 12%-15% to Jio Platforms. According to the brokerage report, “We believe Bharti’s current valuation discount to JPL is unjustified and expect this gap to narrow, at minimum, once JPL goes public.” ALSO READJio IPO: 2 special Investor categories every retail buyer must know Nomura expects the public listing to put greater focus on Jio's earnings growth. With subscriber additions potentially becoming harder to sustain, tariff increases could play a bigger role in driving revenue and profitability. Why Nomura prefers Bharti Airtel Nomura identifies Bharti Airtel as its preferred stock in the telecom sector. Its reasoning centres on the company's subscriber mix and its ability to benefit from potential tariff increases. The brokerage believes Bharti Airtel has a higher proportion of premium subscribers. This could help it manage customer downgrades and subscriber losses when telecom operators raise tariffs. The report also looks at the previous tariff increase in July 2024, when Bharti Airtel recorded the strongest average revenue per user (ARPU) growth among peers, followed by Jio. ARPU measures the average revenue earned per subscriber. Nomura attributed Jio's relatively weaker performance partly to downgrades among its value-conscious customers, including users who do not consume mobile data. What investors need to watch The reported Jio IPO price band remains subject to confirmation by the company. Its final valuation could influence how investors assess Reliance Industries and other telecom stocks. The key factors to track include Jio's final IPO pricing, its earnings growth after listing, the timing of tariff increases and Bharti Airtel's ability to retain premium subscribers. docs.title: Defending the rupee
docs.text:
Sign In 
 CLOSE 
 For uninterrupted reading, switch to App
 READ IN APP 
 Written by The Financial Express 
 Updated: October 13, 2026 07:38 IST 
 Follow Us 
 Unable to arrest the rupee ‘s depreciation through currency-market interventions, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has moved to curb dollar demand and speculation. It has tightened rules governing foreign exchange derivatives: contracts cannot be cancelled and rebooked, positions exceeding $5 million must have an underlying exposure, and banks must set aside 20% of the value of contracts exceeding $2 million in cash. Banks must also ensure that the same exposure is not hedged through multiple dealers. Together with a special dollar window for state-owned oil marketing companies, these constitute perhaps the strongest defence of the currency since 2013. Despite its assertions that it does not defend the rupee at any particular level, the RBI’s latest moves suggest that a sharp depreciation is unacceptable. The dollar’s approach towards `97 appears to have prompted the intervention, making that level a possible line in the sand.
At last Wednesday’s post-monetary policy press conference, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra maintained that the rupee was not overvalued, citing the real effective exchange rate, and observed that markets could be “irrational” in the short run. However, the central bank’s efforts to stem the slide have been undermined by rising US Treasury yields, elevated oil prices, and foreign portfolio outflows. The rupee’s fall to 96.73 against the dollar last Friday, close to its record low of 96.82, appears to have triggered the latest measures. The over 40% surge in Brent crude since the start of the Iran war, accompanied by a roughly 5% depreciation of the rupee, has compounded India’s external vulnerabilities. A weaker currency raises the import bill and fuels inflation, particularly with crude above $100 a barrel and uncertainty over Russian oil supplies. This could force the RBI to tighten monetary policy more aggressively, eventually hurting credit growth.
The restrictions should deter speculation and make it harder to circumvent hedging rules. Importers will face tighter requirements for hedging current-account exposures, although the restrictions do not apply to foreign portfolio investors. Hedging costs, estimated to rise by 80-150 basis points from the prevailing 3.5%, should discourage excessive derivative positions. The special dollar window for oil marketing companies should also reduce demand in the spot market. Earlier this year, the RBI capped banks’ daily net open rupee positions at $100 million and restricted their participation in rupee non-deliverable forwards. Clearly, with the global environment turning adverse, the central bank is unwilling to risk another disorderly depreciation. Although foreign currency reserves have reportedly been bolstered by $142 billion in foreign currency non-resident ( bank ) deposits and foreign currency borrowings, sustained dollar sales could quickly erode these buffers without necessarily reversing the rupee’s trajectory.
The rupee sprang back to an intra-day high of 95.77 against the dollar on Monday, suggesting the measures have had the desired immediate impact. But administrative restrictions and market interventions can only buy time. Elevated oil prices, a strong dollar and persistent capital outflows will continue to weigh on the currency.Unless the global environment improves and India’s trade deficit narrows, the rupee will remain vulnerable to renewed selling. Some fiscal measures, including higher retail fuel prices to contain demand, may become necessary. Further monetary tightening to anchor inflation expectations and measures to attract durable capital inflows may also be required. The RBI has demonstrated its determination to prevent a sharp slide in the rupee. Sustaining that defence, however, will depend as much on developments beyond India’s borders as on its own policy actions.

docs.title: Rs 34,200 cr Kavach opportunity: 2 railway safety stocks to watch as India upgrades its network
docs.text: India’s railway safety upgrade could create a sizeable opportunity for companies working on Kavach. The addressable broad-gauge network alone spans 81,000 route kilometres, representing an estimated ₹34,200 crore opportunity. Another 3,300 route kilometres lie across Dedicated Freight Corridors. But the rollout is far from over. Indian Railways plans to tender Kavach installation across another 41,000 route kilometres between FY27 and FY29. Demand also extends to new locomotives, with regulations requiring every newly manufactured locomotive to be equipped with Kavach before commissioning. With Indian Railways adding around five locomotives a day, or more than 1,900 a year, this requirement adds another source of demand for Kavach suppliers. Against this backdrop, this article examines two specialised players in rail-technology and safety equipment. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Kernex Microsystems: Riding India’s Kavach Revolution Kernex Microsystems is a rail-technology and safety systems company. The company designs, develops, and executes safety-critical railway electronics, signalling, and turnkey infrastructure projects. In turnkey projects, it delivers complete project lifecycle execution, from survey and design to installation. RDSO SIL-4 Certification Drives High-Volume Kavach Rollout The company can produce 6,000 Loco Kavach units, 1,000 Station Kavach units, 500 Remote Interface Units, and 120 Level Crossing Gates (scalable to 300) annually. Kernex is the first OEM to commercially operate Kavach on Vande Bharat trainsets and the first to interface with four different Electronic Interlocking systems. ₹5,174-Crore Order Book Locks in Visible Revenue Through FY29 Kernex holds a total Kavach contract portfolio of ₹5,174 crore (inclusive of GST). To date, ₹1,687 crore (33%) has been executed, leaving a balance order book of ₹3,487 crore (67%). For the FY27-29 horizon, Kernex's cumulative executable base builds to ₹6,727 crore. This comprises ₹2,105 crore projected for FY27, ₹2,200 crore for FY28, and ₹2,422 crore for FY29. An additional ₹2,420 crore from these contract awards is projected to be executed from FY30 onwards. The executable base highlights the monetary value of work scheduled to be executed into revenue over a given financial period. Kernex holds RDSO approval for Kavach Version 4.0 under SIL 4 safety standards, placing it within a limited set of certified suppliers. Post-Commissioning AMCs: The 37x Recurring Cash Flow Engine Kavach deployment also offers a multi-decadal recurring income opportunity. Beyond the initial equipment installation, long-term revenue streams are generated through software upgrades, hardware modifications, and Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMCs). Management projects the AMC revenues alone to grow from ₹5 crore in FY27 to ₹185 crore in FY29. Non-Rail Diversification and ₹150-Crore Global Pipeline Take Shape To expand beyond the core business of railway signalling, Kernex is diversifying into adjacent critical-infrastructure sectors. These comprise Yard Management Systems, Intelligent Traffic Management, Data Centres & Disaster Recovery, and Simulators. Internationally, the company is targeting a ₹150 crore export opportunity over the next two years. ALSO READSunil Singhania’s Rs 266 cr bet, Madhu Kela’s 20x order-book play – stocks up 100%+ Q1 Operating Margins Expand to 32.3% as Operating Leverage Kicks In Financially, consolidated revenue surged to ₹504 crore in Q1FY27, up from ₹56 crore in Q1FY26. EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortisation) rose to ₹163 crore from ₹10 crore in Q1FY26, while margin stood at 32.3%. Net profit surged to ₹110 crore, up from ₹7 crore in Q1FY26. Order book execution remains the key going ahead. Q1FY27 earnings are yet to be announced. Kernex Share Price #2 Concord Control Systems: Beyond Kavach, Building the Future of Rail Safety Concord Control Systems is a railway technology platform company. It develops mission-critical electronics, safety systems, propulsion technologies, and diagnostic solutions. It is an approved OEM and vendor for Indian Railways bodies, including the RDSO, Chittaranjan Locomotive Works, and Integral Coach Factory. RDSO Vendor Status and Vertical Supply Chain Integration Concord participates in the Kavach program through Progota, in which it holds a 46.5% stake. It operates as an indigenous R&D player developing proprietary technology in-house. Through its backward integration with Fusion Electronics (PCBs and box-build solutions) and Advanced Rail Controls, it benefits from cost efficiencies and vertical integration for its Kavach hardware. Concord's Kavach suite includes both onboard locomotive hardware and control infrastructure. Concord secured ₹258.3 crore in total Kavach orders during FY26. This includes major contract wins of ₹185.1 crore and ₹53.7 crore for on-board Kavach 4.0 equipment. The execution timeline is 12 months. ₹697-Crore Order Book Underpins 3.3x Revenue Visibility Concord closed FY26 with an executable order book of ₹697 crore, up 228% year-on-year. This order provides 3.3x revenue visibility relative to FY26 revenue of ₹210 crore. Following its 80% acquisition, Fusion Electronics is expected to become a direct revenue contributor in FY27. The Kavach platform yields 25-30% EBITDA margins and generates long-term recurring revenue through 15-year maintenance contracts. Looking ahead, management is guiding for a 40% to 50% revenue CAGR over the coming years. Management maintains a sustainable baseline target of 22% to 25% EBITDA margins. Expanding Into 15-Year Maintenance and Digital Signalling Assets By FY30, management aims to shift a significant portion of its revenue from one-off equipment manufacturing to high-margin, annuity-based streams. This includes AMCs, software licenses, diagnostics analytics, and IP royalties
